William Crookes discovered the phenomenon of cathode rays in 1869-1875, while experimenting with early discharge tubes. These experiments led to the discovery of X-rays by Wilhelm Röntgen in 1895 when he applied a similar type of tube called a Crookes tube for producing radiography and discovered that X-rays are produced when electrons collide at high energies with atoms in matter.

These were first observed around 1869-1875 by English physicist William Crookes and others experimenting with early discharge tubes to measure current, voltage, temperature, pressure, etc., while varying the filament material.

The discovery of X-rays was a major scientific breakthrough that led to important applications in medicine, including radiography. Today, the term "Crookes tube" is also used for the first generation cold cathode X-ray tubes developed from the experimental Crookes tubes and first used until about 1920 by various researchers.

It's worth noting that while Crookes was initially working on the development of electric lighting using vacuum arc lamps, his experiments with gases led to the discovery of cathode rays, which later became known as electron beams. The term "Crookes tube" came into use when the experimental tubes evolved into production X-ray tubes used in industry and medicine.

The first generation of cold cathode X-ray tubes is also sometimes called a Crookes tube since they were developed from an earlier type experimentally produced by Crookes, Hittorf, Plücker, Goldstein, Lenard, Birkeland and others. These experimental tubes provided the basis for further development of modern X-ray tubes that are used in medicine to produce radiography images.

It's also worth mentioning that Wilhelm Röntgen was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901 "in recognition of his services to the advance of chemistry by the introduction of X-rays in his investigations into the internal structure of metals and of substances of similar composition," for which he is often associated with discovery of X-rays. The term "Röntgen" was later also adopted as an adjective to describe objects that can be seen clearly on a radiograph, such as bones.

The Rosetta Stone is a stele of granodiorite inscribed with three versions of a decree issued in 196 BC during the Ptolemaic dynasty of Egypt, on behalf of King Ptolemy V Epiphanes. The top and middle texts are in Ancient Egyptian using hieroglyphic and Demotic scripts, respectively, while the bottom is in Ancient Greek.

The stone was carved during the Hellenistic period and is believed to have originally been displayed within a temple, possibly at Sais. It was probably moved in late antiquity or during the Mamluk period, and was eventually used as building material in the construction of Fort Julien near the town of Rashid (Rosetta) in the Nile Delta.

It was found there in July 1799 by French army officer Pierre-François Bouchard during France's invasion of Egypt. It was the first Ancient Egyptian bilingual text recovered in modern times, and it aroused widespread public interest with its potential to decipher this previously untranslated hieroglyphic script. Lithographic copies and plaster casts soon began circulating among European museums and schools.

Nikola Tesla was an inventor and electrical engineer who made significant contributions to the development of the global electric power system. He is known for his work on alternating current (AC) systems, which revolutionized electricity distribution and transmission. Tesla also designed early versions of radio transmitters and receivers.

The Nikola Tesla Museum in Belgrade, Serbia, is dedicated to honoring and displaying the life and work of Nikola Tesla as well as the final resting place for him.
